title: Genomic DNA Extraction (General Workflow)

references.label: General microbiology/molecular biology laboratory manuals (ASM curriculum resources)

purpose: To isolate genomic DNA from cells or tissue in a form pure and intact enough for downstream applications such as PCR, restriction digestion, or sequencing.
principle: Cells are lysed to release their contents, proteins and other cellular debris are removed (through enzymatic digestion, salting-out, or binding to a silica matrix depending on the specific method), and the purified DNA is recovered by precipitation or elution, leaving behind RNA (if not also digested), protein, and lipid contaminants.
requiredReagents: Lysis buffer (typically containing a detergent to disrupt membranes)
RNase A (if RNA-free DNA is required)
Wash and elution buffers appropriate to the extraction method (column-based, salting-out, or organic extraction)

procedure.instruction: Pellet or collect the starting cell/tissue material and resuspend in lysis buffer containing detergent and proteinase K.
Incubate at the manufacturer- or method-specified temperature and time to allow complete cell lysis and protein digestion.
If RNA-free DNA is required, treat with RNase A per the method's instructions.
Remove protein and other contaminants using the chosen method's separation step (e.g. binding DNA to a silica column and washing, or a salting-out/precipitation step for non-column methods).
Elute or resuspend the purified DNA in an appropriate low-salt buffer or nuclease-free water.
Quantify yield and assess purity (commonly via A260 and the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios) before proceeding to downstream applications.

observations: A260-based concentration reading appropriate for the intended downstream use.
A260/A280 ratio near 1.8, consistent with low protein contamination.
interpretation: Adequate yield combined with acceptable purity ratios indicates DNA suitable for most downstream molecular applications; low yield may reflect insufficient starting material or incomplete lysis, while poor purity ratios point to incomplete removal of protein or other contaminants.
criticalNotes: Avoid vigorous vortexing of extracted genomic DNA, which can shear it into smaller fragments than intended for applications requiring high-molecular-weight DNA.
Ensure complete lysis and protein digestion before proceeding — incomplete lysis is a common cause of low yield.
precautions: Handle proteinase K and lysis reagents per their safety data sheets.
Use nuclease-free consumables and reagents to avoid degrading the extracted DNA.
biosafetyNotes: Handle starting material (cells/tissue) per its specific biosafety risk assessment through the lysis step.
limitations: Extraction efficiency and purity vary meaningfully by starting material type (e.g. Gram-positive bacteria with thick cell walls, versus mammalian tissue) and may require method-specific modification.
Some extraction methods do not fully remove PCR inhibitors even when purity ratios look acceptable.
